lessons.subject: Data Processing
lessons.title: The input, processing and output flow the scheme draws twice in Week 1, given as a readable ordered relationship
objectives: State the three-stage flow of Week 1 in order and give it as readable text, with the scheme line that supports each stage
Say what survived extraction of the two drawings and what this representation therefore does not claim
Give both occurrences of the flow, record that they are copies of one flow, and keep them apart from the six-stage cycle
lessons.body:
THE FLOW THE SCHEME DRAWS TWICE: INPUT, THEN PROCESSING, THEN OUTPUT

What you will learn: the three-stage flow that Week 1 of the Data Processing scheme draws twice, set out here as readable text; what survived when the document was read, what did not survive, and therefore what this lesson does not claim; and how the flow differs from the six-stage cycle that the same week lists.

This lesson disposes of a diagram. The scheme drew the flow twice with arrow shapes placed inside the text, not as a picture, so no image has ever existed to recover. What is delivered below is the ordered relationship in words, with the line of the scheme that supports each stage. No render of the source page is committed, no picture has been redrawn, and no measurement of the original arrows is claimed as recovered.

1. THE RELATIONSHIP, WRITTEN OUT

INPUT -> PROCESSING -> OUTPUT

The three words are the scheme's own labels. The arrows between them are the part that was lost, so the reading of the order is stated here from what does survive: the labels stand in that sequence in both copies, and the sentences around them spell the same order out.

First stage - INPUT. The basic facts are put in. Line 97 introduces data as any basic fact that may be fed into some processing system, so entering is what happens to data first.
Second stage - PROCESSING. The facts are worked over. The same line describes a processing system as one doing computation, comparison and general manipulation of the data, and says the work may be done by people or by a machine, naming the computer as its own example.
Third stage - OUTPUT. What comes out is information. Line 101 treats information as the result a processing system ends with, and adds that management needs it in order to decide.

Line 101 also announces that the pairing of data with information is what the drawing beneath it exhibits, and line 175 states the same three-part structure in ordinary prose: most of this work, it says, can be looked at as data, a processor and an output. The same three words return, in the same order, as the headings of the week's activity list at lines 191 to 195, so the sequence is the scheme's own and not one supplied here.

2. THE TWO COPIES ARE ONE FLOW

The scheme puts this flow on the page twice in Week 1, and the two copies are the same three stages. The first is at line 105, inside the paragraph that is the 51st direct child of the document body; its labels are held apart by tabbing, and a page division follows it. The second is at line 169, inside the paragraph that is the 83rd direct child, standing under the element sentence at line 167; its labels are held apart by spacing, and extraction presses PROCESSING and OUTPUT together into one word.

Both paragraphs carry two arrow shapes each, of the one straight-arrow kind the document uses, and nothing else in the document uses that kind. Neither paragraph carries image data of any sort, which is why the flow was never a picture. Counting the copies as two, and the arrow shapes as four, is a record of what the source holds; it is not a claim that two different flows are taught.

3. WHAT THIS LESSON DOES NOT CLAIM

It does not present a diagram. The readable line in section 1 is a substitute for the drawing, chosen because the owner's brief asks for readable text in preference to a new image asset, and it may not be reported as a delivered picture.
It does not report the geometry of the arrows. Their placement data sits in the document markup but is not reproduced, measured or turned into a claim about the drawing, because the extracted text of the scheme carries no such information.
It does not add a stage. Nothing beyond the three labels has been placed in the flow, so no fourth stage appears in it.
It does not absorb two neighbouring topics. Storage is named at line 175 as something that usually also features, and the six-stage cycle listed at lines 149 to 163 is a separate teaching point of the same week; both are kept out of this three-stage flow, and neither is closed here.

4. WHAT STILL HAS TO BE DELIVERED

Week 1 has no lesson of its own yet apart from this supplement, so nothing in the week is deliverable: 11 teaching sections stay PARTIAL and 6 assessment or reading sections stay UNRESOLVED, and the coverage entry for this flow is equivalent rather than supported, because what is delivered is the relationship and not the author's drawing. Two blockers stay open - the week has no authored lessons, and the flow is still not a delivered diagram. The lesson tasks of the queue (manual with versus electronic processing, the properties and the cycle, the assessment key, and the computer-as-tool item) are untouched by this work.

5. HOW TO WORK WITH THIS FLOW

Write the three stages in order and say, for each one, which line of the scheme puts it there. Then say what the drawing was made of and what happened to it when the document was read as text, so that a reader knows this order is a reconstruction from labels and prose rather than a recovered picture. Keep the cycle of lines 149 to 163 for its own lesson; the two lists answer different questions and merging them would teach stages the labels do not hold.

practice.question: Write out, in order, the three-stage flow that Week 1 draws twice, and give the scheme line that supports each stage.
practice.answer:
INPUT -> PROCESSING -> OUTPUT
INPUT - line 97, which presents data as any basic fact that may be fed into a processing system.
PROCESSING - line 97, which describes the system as doing computation, comparison and manipulation of the data.
OUTPUT - line 101, which makes information the result a processing system ends with.

practice.question: What survived when the two drawings were read out of the document, and what did not? Say what the delivered text is therefore not.
practice.answer: The three labels survived as text; the arrow shapes did not. Each copy was drawn with two straight arrow shapes placed in the paragraph rather than as an image, and neither paragraph holds image data, so there was never a picture to extract. The order is read from the label sequence and from the sentences around it, not from recovered geometry. practice.question: Where do the two copies of the flow appear, and what is their relationship to one another?
practice.answer: At line 105, in the 51st direct child paragraph of the document body, with its labels held apart by tabbing and a page division after it; and at line 169, in the 83rd direct child paragraph, standing under the element sentence at line 167, where extraction presses PROCESSING and OUTPUT together. They are two copies of one and the same flow: the same three stages, different spacing, different digests. Each copy holds two arrow shapes of the same straight-arrow kind, and those four shapes are the only ones of that kind in the document.

marking.criterion: Both occurrences given with their locators (line 105 and line 169)
Recorded as duplicates of one flow rather than two different flows
Notes that the second copy loses the space between PROCESSING and OUTPUT

practice.question: Is this flow the same thing as the data processing cycle of the same week? Say how the two are kept apart here.
practice.answer: No. The flow above is the three labels of lines 105 and 169 and nothing else. The cycle is a separate list at lines 149 to 163, carrying a framing sentence and six stage labels. Storage appears in that cycle list and is separately named at line 175 as something that usually also features, but it is not a fourth stage of this flow, and no stage has been added to the flow from the cycle. The cycle itself stays open for its own lesson.

Gives the cycle locator (lines 149 to 163) or its six labels
